### Moderator Analysis

Even though heterogeneity was not detected among the included studies, as previous literature suggested, methodological differences could influence the effect of interventions on SRC outcomes \[ [27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR27 "Borenstein M, Hedges LV, Higgins JP, Rothstein HR. Therefore, moderator analyses were performed to investigate the potential impact of intervention type (physical- vs. educational-based) and context of athletic exposure (practice vs. match) on the overall effect. No statistical significance was found for either of the moderator variables, indicating that neither intervention type nor athletic exposure context had a significant influence on the overall effect of the interventions, as displayed in Table [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#Tab5). ## Discussion

The current meta-analysis investigated the efficacy of SRC injury prevention programs in reducing the incidence rates of SRC, while also exploring whether their efficacy varied based on the type of intervention and the context of athletic exposure. The results indicated that, overall, injury prevention programs can reduce SRC incidence rates by 34%. This substantial reduction in SRC injury rates represents promising evidence for ongoing efforts to mitigate risks associated with SRC. Furthermore, the preventive efficacy is not influenced by intervention type (physical- vs. educational-based) or the athletic exposure context (practice vs. match).

Compared with other intervention strategies, the efficacy of injury prevention programs identified in this meta-analysis was second only to policy changes. Eliason et al. \[ [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR13 "Eliason PH, Galarneau J-M, Kolstad AT, Pankow MP, West SW, Bailey S, et al. Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(12):749–61.")\] reported that mouthguard use in collision sports reduced SRC risk by 26%. Disallowing bodychecking in youth ice hockey led to a 58% reduction, and limiting contact during American Football practices reduced SRCs by 64% \[ [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR13 "Eliason PH, Galarneau J-M, Kolstad AT, Pankow MP, West SW, Bailey S, et al. Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(12):749–61.")\]. Since the majority of SRCs occur as a result of player contact \[ [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR30 "Zuckerman SL, Kerr ZY, Yengo-Kahn A, Wasserman E, Covassin T, Solomon GS. Epidemiology of sports-related concussion in NCAA athletes from 2009–2010 to 2013–2014: incidence, recurrence, and mechanisms. Am J Sports Med. 2015;43(11):2654–62.")\], disallowing or limiting contact is arguably the most direct and effective preventive strategy. The preventive effect of mouthguards on SRC remains inconclusive \[ [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR13 "Eliason PH, Galarneau J-M, Kolstad AT, Pankow MP, West SW, Bailey S, et al. Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(12):749–61."), [37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR37 "Knapik JJ, Hoedebecke BL, Rogers GG, Sharp MA, Marshall SW. Effectiveness of mouthguards for the prevention of orofacial injuries and concussions in sports: systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2019;49:1217–32.")\]. Although a 26% reduction was observed in a pooled analysis \[ [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR13 "Eliason PH, Galarneau J-M, Kolstad AT, Pankow MP, West SW, Bailey S, et al. Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(12):749–61.")\], the estimate was heavily influenced by a single study in ice hockey, which accounted for 83% of the total weight \[ [38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR38 "Chisholm DA, Black AM, Palacios-Derflingher L, Eliason PH, Schneider KJ, Emery CA, et al. Mouthguard use in youth ice hockey and the risk of concussion: nested case–control study of 315 cases. Br J Sports Med. 2020;54(14):866–70.")\], potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings. Moreover, another meta-analysis found no significant difference in SRC incidence between athletes who wore mouthguards and those who did not \[ [37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR37 "Knapik JJ, Hoedebecke BL, Rogers GG, Sharp MA, Marshall SW. Effectiveness of mouthguards for the prevention of orofacial injuries and concussions in sports: systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2019;49:1217–32.")\], further underscoring the uncertainty surrounding their effectiveness in SRC prevention. Therefore, in addition to policy changes, injury prevention programs represent a practical and effective strategy for reducing the risk of SRC.

Unexpectedly, we found that the efficacy of SRC injury prevention programs in reducing SRC is not influenced by the type of intervention. Notably, our finidings demonstrated a 39% reduction in SRC incidence rate associated with physical training-based injury prevention programs (IRR = 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.89), although the reduction was not statistically significant. Physical training-based injury prevention programs implemented in the included studies could be categorized into multicomponent exercise programs \[ [20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR20 "Attwood MJ, Roberts SP, Trewartha G, England ME, Stokes KA. Efficacy of a movement control injury prevention programme in adult men’s community rugby union: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):368–74."), [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR21 "Barden C, Hancock MV, Stokes KA, Roberts SP, McKay CD. Effectiveness of the activate injury prevention exercise programme to prevent injury in schoolboy rugby union. Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(14):812–7."), [22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR22 "Hislop MD, Stokes KA, Williams S, McKay CD, England ME, Kemp SPT, et al. Reducing musculoskeletal injury and concussion risk in schoolboy rugby players with a pre-activity movement control exercise programme: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(15):1140–6."), [36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR36 "Obërtinca R, Meha R, Hoxha I, Shabani B, Meyer T, Aus der Fünten K. Efficacy of a new injury prevention programme (FUNBALL) in young male football (soccer) players: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2024;58(10):548–55.")\] and neck muscle training programs \[ [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR17 "Gillies L, McKay M, Kertanegara S, Huertas N, Nutt S, Peek K. The implementation of a neck strengthening exercise program in elite rugby union: A team case study over one season. Phys Ther Sport. 2022 2022/5//;55:248 – 55."), [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR18 "Peek K, Versteegh T, Veith S, Whalan M, Edwards S, McKay M, et al. Injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and the incidence of soccer-related head and neck injuries. J Athl Train. 2023;58(6):519–27.")\] (Table [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#Tab6)). Multicomponent exercise programs encompass a variety of exercises aimed at enhancing different aspects of physical ability (e.g., strength, power, or balance) and are typically implemented during pre-game warm-ups \[ [20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR20 "Attwood MJ, Roberts SP, Trewartha G, England ME, Stokes KA. Efficacy of a movement control injury prevention programme in adult men’s community rugby union: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):368–74."), [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR21 "Barden C, Hancock MV, Stokes KA, Roberts SP, McKay CD. Effectiveness of the activate injury prevention exercise programme to prevent injury in schoolboy rugby union. Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(14):812–7."), [22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR22 "Hislop MD, Stokes KA, Williams S, McKay CD, England ME, Kemp SPT, et al. Reducing musculoskeletal injury and concussion risk in schoolboy rugby players with a pre-activity movement control exercise programme: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(15):1140–6."), [36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR36 "Obërtinca R, Meha R, Hoxha I, Shabani B, Meyer T, Aus der Fünten K. Efficacy of a new injury prevention programme (FUNBALL) in young male football (soccer) players: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2024;58(10):548–55.")\]. Conversely, neck muscle training programs specifically target the neck musculature and are often incorporated into regular training routines \[ [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR17 "Gillies L, McKay M, Kertanegara S, Huertas N, Nutt S, Peek K. The implementation of a neck strengthening exercise program in elite rugby union: A team case study over one season. Phys Ther Sport. 2022 2022/5//;55:248 – 55."), [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR18 "Peek K, Versteegh T, Veith S, Whalan M, Edwards S, McKay M, et al. The observed reduction in SRC incidence rate following physical training interventions may be attributed to improvements in neck strength and balance/dynamic stability. In the six studies with physical training-based programs included in our review, five incorporated neck strength training (Table [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#Tab6)). SRCs can result from a direct blow to the head or body contact that transmits inertial impulse forces through the neck to the head \[ [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR6 "Patricios JS, Schneider KJ, Dvorak J, Ahmed OH, Blauwet C, Cantu RC, et al. Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport–Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(11):695–711."), [39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR39 "Elliott J, Heron N, Versteegh T, Gilchrist IA, Webb M, Archbold P, et al. Injury reduction programs for reducing the incidence of sport-related head and neck injuries including concussion: a systematic review. Sports Med. 2021;51(11):2373–88.")\]. Enhanced neck strength may mitigate the risk of SRC by improving stability between the trunk, neck, and head \[ [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR40 "Garrett JM, Mastrorocco M, Peek K, Van den Hoek DJ, McGuckian TB. The relationship between neck strength and sports-related concussion in team sports: a systematic review with meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Therapy. 2023;53(10):585–93.")\]. This improved coupling helps stabilize the head during impacts, such as head-on-body collisions in rugby or head-to-head impacts in soccer \[ [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR40 "Garrett JM, Mastrorocco M, Peek K, Van den Hoek DJ, McGuckian TB. The relationship between neck strength and sports-related concussion in team sports: a systematic review with meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Therapy. 2023;53(10):585–93.")\]. Enhanced stability may also aid in dissipating the impact forces transmitted to the brain, thereby reducing the risk of SRC \[ [22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR22 "Hislop MD, Stokes KA, Williams S, McKay CD, England ME, Kemp SPT, et al. Reducing musculoskeletal injury and concussion risk in schoolboy rugby players with a pre-activity movement control exercise programme: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(15):1140–6.")\]. In fact, athletes with greater neck strength experience lower magnitudes of head impacts in team sports \[ [40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR40 "Garrett JM, Mastrorocco M, Peek K, Van den Hoek DJ, McGuckian TB. The relationship between neck strength and sports-related concussion in team sports: a systematic review with meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Therapy. 2023;53(10):585–93.")\]. Moreover, in male professional rugby players, low neck extension strength has been identified as a risk factor for SRCs, with a 10% increase in neck extensor strength associated with a 13% decrease in the incidence rate of SRCs \[ [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR11 "Farley T, Barry E, Sylvester R, De Medici A, Wilson MG. Poor isometric neck extension strength as a risk factor for concussion in male professional rugby union players. Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(11):616–21.")\]. Integrating neuromuscular neck exercises into the FIFA 11 + program has been also shown to reduce head acceleration during headers and lower the risk of diagnosed SRCs among adolescent soccer players \[ [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR18 "Peek K, Versteegh T, Veith S, Whalan M, Edwards S, McKay M, et al. Injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and the incidence of soccer-related head and neck injuries. J Athl Train. 2023;58(6):519–27."), [41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR41 "Peek K, Andersen J, McKay MJ, Versteegh T, Gilchrist IA, Meyer T, et al. The effect of the FIFA 11 + with added neck exercises on maximal isometric neck strength and peak head impact magnitude during heading: a pilot study. Sports Med. 2022.                    https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01564-0                                    .")\]. Neck muscle training is likely a critical component contributing to the efficacy of physical training-based programs in reducing SRC rates. In addition, balance and dynamic stability training appear to be also vital for SRC prevention. Poor balance can impair a player’s motor control and body awareness, leading to suboptimal tackle techniques and an increased risk of SRC \[ [42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR42 "Johnston, O’Reilly M, Duignan C, Liston M, McLoughlin R, Coughlan GF, et al. Association of dynamic balance with Sports-Related concussion: A prospective cohort study. Am J Sports Med. 2019;47(1):197–205.")\]. For instance, a previous study reported that rugby players exhibiting poor dynamic balance have a threefold higher risk of sustaining a SRC, even when accounting for concussion history \[ [42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR42 "Johnston, O’Reilly M, Duignan C, Liston M, McLoughlin R, Coughlan GF, et al. Association of dynamic balance with Sports-Related concussion: A prospective cohort study. Am J Sports Med. 2019;47(1):197–205.")\]. Given the established connection between poor dynamic balance and a higher risk of SRC, alongside the fact that four out of six physical training-based studies included balance or dynamic stability exercises, it is crucial to incorporate such training into SRC prevention programs.

Concussion safety education commonly aims to equip athletes with the knowledge and skills necessary to effectively manage situations that might lead to SRCs. According to our findings, educational-based injury prevention programs implemented in two of the included studies can reduce the SRC incidence rates by 24%, although this reduction was not statistically significant (IRR 0.76; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.30). Notably, both included studies implemented the HUF program \[ [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR24 "Shanley E, Thigpen C, Kissenberth M, Gilliland RG, Thorpe J, Nance D, et al. Heads up football training decreases concussion rates in high school football players. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(2):120–6."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR26 "Kerr ZY, Yeargin S, Valovich McLeod TC, Nittoli VC, Mensch J, Dodge T, et al. Comprehensive coach education and practice contact restriction guidelines result in lower injury rates in youth American football. Orthop J Sports Med. 2015;3(7):2325967115594578.")\], an intervention focused on comprehensive coach education and contact training designed to enhance the safety of American Football players during practice and matches \[ [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR13 "Eliason PH, Galarneau J-M, Kolstad AT, Pankow MP, West SW, Bailey S, et al. Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(12):749–61."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR26 "Kerr ZY, Yeargin S, Valovich McLeod TC, Nittoli VC, Mensch J, Dodge T, et al. Comprehensive coach education and practice contact restriction guidelines result in lower injury rates in youth American football. Orthop J Sports Med. 2015;3(7):2325967115594578.")\]. However, two studies, in fact, yielded conflicting results. Shanley et al. reported that the HUF program reduced SRC incidence rate during practices by 47% (IRR 0.53; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.93)) \[ [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR24 "Shanley E, Thigpen C, Kissenberth M, Gilliland RG, Thorpe J, Nance D, et al. Heads up football training decreases concussion rates in high school football players. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(2):120–6.")\], while Kerr et al. found no significant difference in SRC injury rates following HUF program implementation during either practices or matches \[ [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR26 "Kerr ZY, Yeargin S, Valovich McLeod TC, Nittoli VC, Mensch J, Dodge T, et al. Comprehensive coach education and practice contact restriction guidelines result in lower injury rates in youth American football. Orthop J Sports Med. 2015;3(7):2325967115594578.")\]. A key distinction between the two studies was the implementation of a fidelity audit schedule in Shanley et al.'s study \[ [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR24 "Shanley E, Thigpen C, Kissenberth M, Gilliland RG, Thorpe J, Nance D, et al. Heads up football training decreases concussion rates in high school football players. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(2):120–6.")\], which was absent in Kerr et al.'s study \[ [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR26 "Kerr ZY, Yeargin S, Valovich McLeod TC, Nittoli VC, Mensch J, Dodge T, et al. Comprehensive coach education and practice contact restriction guidelines result in lower injury rates in youth American football. Orthop J Sports Med. 2015;3(7):2325967115594578.")\]. The fidelity audit ensured that schools participating in the study were assessed for compliance with heads-up techniques during all contact drills in at least three monitored practice sessions \[ [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR24 "Shanley E, Thigpen C, Kissenberth M, Gilliland RG, Thorpe J, Nance D, et al. Heads up football training decreases concussion rates in high school football players. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(2):120–6.")\]. Previous research has emphasized the critical role of supervision in ensuring adherence to safety protocols \[ [25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR25 "Kerr ZY, Dalton SL, Roos KG, Djoko A, Phelps J, Dompier TP. Comparison of Indiana high school football injury rates by inclusion of the USA football heads up football player safety coach. Orthop J Sports Med 2016 2016/5//;4(5):1-.")\]. High school teams with a player safety coach overseeing compliance with HUF protocols experienced lower injury and SRC rates during practice compared to teams that implemented HUF without such oversight \[ [25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR25 "Kerr ZY, Dalton SL, Roos KG, Djoko A, Phelps J, Dompier TP. Comparison of Indiana high school football injury rates by inclusion of the USA football heads up football player safety coach. Orthop J Sports Med 2016 2016/5//;4(5):1-.")\]. This suggests that while the HUF program is a potentially effective educational-based SRC injury prevention intervention, proper supervision may be essential for ensuring adherence.

Key components of the HUF program related to SRC risk reduction include hands-on training in equipment fitting, strategies to minimize player-to-player contact, and teaching proper tackling techniques \[ [43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR43 "Kerr ZY, Kroshus E, Lee JG, Yeargin SW, Dompier TP. Coaches’ implementation of the USA football heads up football educational program. Health Promot Pract. 2018;19(2):184–93.")\]. For instance, having thicker padding over the zygoma and mandible area may reduce SRC incidence rates in American Football \[ [44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR44 "Collins M, Lovell MR, Iverson GL, Ide T, Maroon J. Examining concussion rates and return to play in high school football players wearing newer helmet technology: a three-year prospective cohort study. Neurosurgery. 2006;58(2):275–86."), [45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR45 "Rowson S, Duma SM, Greenwald RM, Beckwith JG, Chu JJ, Guskiewicz KM, et al. Can helmet design reduce the risk of concussion in football? J Neurosurg. 2014;120(4):919–22.")\], and inadequate helmet fit can increase SRC rates in ice hockey \[ [46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR46 "Gamble AS, Bigg JL, Sick S, Krolikowski M, Patton DA, Hagel BE, et al. Helmet fit assessment and concussion risk in youth ice hockey players: a nested case-control study. J Athl Train. 2021;56(8):845–50.")\]. Alongside this, player-to-player contact accounts for the majority of SRCs in collegiate and elite-level female soccer (80–91%) \[ [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR14 "Pankow MP, Syrydiuk R, Kolstad A, Hayden A, Dennison C, Mrazik M, et al. Head games: a systematic review and meta-analysis examining concussion and head impact incidence rates, modifiable risk factors, and prevention strategies in youth tackle football. Sports Med. 2022;52(6):1259–72.")\], with tackling identified as the most common concussive event in both American Football (37–48%) \[ [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR14 "Pankow MP, Syrydiuk R, Kolstad A, Hayden A, Dennison C, Mrazik M, et al. Head games: a systematic review and meta-analysis examining concussion and head impact incidence rates, modifiable risk factors, and prevention strategies in youth tackle football. Sports Med. 2022;52(6):1259–72.")\] and rugby (58–64%) \[ [11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR11 "Farley T, Barry E, Sylvester R, De Medici A, Wilson MG. Poor isometric neck extension strength as a risk factor for concussion in male professional rugby union players. Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(11):616–21.")\]. Therefore, strategies aimed at reducing player-to-player contact and improving tackling techniques, such as heads-up tackling \[ [47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR47 "Matsuo H, Yamada Y, Masuchi K, Matsumoto T. Effectiveness of the heads up tackling (HUT) program on tackling safety and performance in American football. Int J Sport Health Sci. 2018;16:77–88.")\], may also be crucial in reducing SRC incidence. Although instruction on equipment fitting, strategies to reduce player-to-player contact, and proper tackling techniques within the HUF program may contribute to its efficacy in reducing SRC incidence rates, the current review was limited to studies that compared educational-based SRC injury prevention programs with a control group. This eligibility criteria led to the exclusion of a study that compared educational-based interventions with and without a player safety coach \[ [25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR25 "Kerr ZY, Dalton SL, Roos KG, Djoko A, Phelps J, Dompier TP. Comparison of Indiana high school football injury rates by inclusion of the USA football heads up football player safety coach. Orthop J Sports Med 2016 2016/5//;4(5):1-.")\]. Thus, only two studies (with three data points) were included in the final analysis, both focusing on the HUF program in American Football \[ [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR24 "Shanley E, Thigpen C, Kissenberth M, Gilliland RG, Thorpe J, Nance D, et al. Heads up football training decreases concussion rates in high school football players. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(2):120–6."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR26 "Kerr ZY, Yeargin S, Valovich McLeod TC, Nittoli VC, Mensch J, Dodge T, et al. Comprehensive coach education and practice contact restriction guidelines result in lower injury rates in youth American football. Orthop J Sports Med. 2015;3(7):2325967115594578.")\]. Additional research is necessary to evaluate the efficacy of various educational-based interventions in reducing SRCs across different sports.

An unexpected finding of this study is that while SRC injury prevention programs effectively reduce SRC incidence rates, the athletic exposure context did not significantly moderate SRC incidence. These findings do not support our hypothesis, indicating that the efficacy of injury prevention programs in reducing SRC incidence rate was similar in both match and practice context. One possible explanation is that SRC injury prevention programs enhance athletes’ physical abilities and technical skills, enabling athletes to navigate varying situations associated with SRC across different athletic exposure contexts, leading to comparable efficacy in SRC prevention. This finding contrasts with the work of Nuhu et al., who reported the FIFA 11 + warm-up program reducing injuries by 40% during matches and 30% during practice \[ [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR29 "Nuhu A, Jelsma J, Dunleavy K, Burgess T. Effect of the FIFA 11 + soccer specific warm up programme on the incidence of injuries: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. PLoS ONE. 2021;16(5):e0251839.")\]. The discrepancy may stem from differences in injury definitions; our study focused solely on confirmed SRCs, whereas Nuhu et al. defined injury more broadly as any physical complaint resulting from soccer participation, regardless of whether it occurred in practice or a match \[ [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR29 "Nuhu A, Jelsma J, Dunleavy K, Burgess T. Effect of the FIFA 11 + soccer specific warm up programme on the incidence of injuries: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. PLoS ONE. 2021;16(5):e0251839.")\]. Given that match intensity is typically higher than in practices, the high-intensity environment may lead to a greater variety and severity of injuries \[ [28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR28 "Brito J, Malina RM, Seabra A, Massada JL, Soares JM, Krustrup P, et al. Injuries in Portuguese youth soccer players during training and match play. J Athl Train. 2012;47(2):191–7.")\]. A broader injury definition could exaggerate the difference in the efficacy of injury prevention programs between practices and matches, making the intervention program appear more effective during matches \[ [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR29 "Nuhu A, Jelsma J, Dunleavy K, Burgess T. Effect of the FIFA 11 + soccer specific warm up programme on the incidence of injuries: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. PLoS ONE. 2021;16(5):e0251839.")\]. In contrast, in studies with a clear injury definition, such as that by Soligard et al., which defined an injury as one that prevented a player from fully participating in the next scheduled match or training session, the efficacy of the injury prevention program was, in fact, similar across both contexts, with an incidence rate ratio (IRR) of 0.72 (0.52 to 1.00) for matches and 0.68 (0.41 to 1.11) for practices \[ [48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR48 "Soligard T, Myklebust G, Steffen K, Holme I, Silvers H, Bizzini M, et al. Comprehensive warm-up programme to prevent injuries in young female footballers: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2008.                    https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.a2469                                    .")\]. These discussions highlight the importance of specific injury definitions when evaluating the efficacy of intervention programs. Another potential explanation for this discrepancy may lie in the differences in injury mechanisms. Most SRCs are caused by player contact \[ [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR30 "Zuckerman SL, Kerr ZY, Yengo-Kahn A, Wasserman E, Covassin T, Solomon GS. Epidemiology of sports-related concussion in NCAA athletes from 2009–2010 to 2013–2014: incidence, recurrence, and mechanisms. Am J Sports Med. 2015;43(11):2654–62.")\], whereas injuries such as ACL tears often result from non-contact mechanisms \[ [49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR49 "Mountcastle SB, Posner M, Kragh JF, Taylor DC Jr. Gender differences in anterior cruciate ligament injury vary with activity: epidemiology of anterior cruciate ligament injuries in a young, athletic population. Am J Sports Med. 2007;35(10):1635–42.")\]. Injury prevention programs targeting lower extremity injuries typically focus on enhancing neuromuscular control, balance, and movement patterns during dynamic tasks \[ [50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR50 "Sadigursky D, Braid JA, De Lira DNL, Machado BAB, Carneiro RJF, Colavolpe PO. The FIFA 11 + injury prevention program for soccer players: a systematic review. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2017;9:1–8.")\], and their efficacy may be amplified in higher-intensity match situations. In contrast, for contact-related events, the head impacts that lead to SRCs are unlikely to differ significantly between practice and match, even if their intensity levels vary. Neck strength training is one of the few plausible interventions that may help attenuate head impacts \[ [51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR51 "Caccese JB, Buckley TA, Tierney RT, Arbogast KB, Rose WC, Glutting JJ, et al. Head and neck size and neck strength predict linear and rotational acceleration during purposeful soccer heading. Sports Biomech. 2018;17(4):462–76.")\]; however, only one study within the context-specific subgroup analysis incorporated neck muscle training \[ [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR17 "Gillies L, McKay M, Kertanegara S, Huertas N, Nutt S, Peek K. The implementation of a neck strengthening exercise program in elite rugby union: A team case study over one season. Phys Ther Sport. 2022 2022/5//;55:248 – 55.")\]. Future research is needed to examine whether injury prevention programs that incorporate neck muscle training can differentially reduce the risk of SRC during practice versus match. This may help explain why injury prevention programs demonstrate greater efficacy in reducing broader sport-related injuries during match settings, yet exhibit similar efficacy for SRC across practice and match settings. Nevertheless, our findings are practically meaningful, indicating that consistently implementing targeted training interventions across both matches and practices likely mitigates SRC risks regardless of athletic exposure context.

### Limitations

This review has some limitations. First, the included studies in our review predominantly focused on male participants, with only one study including both male and female subjects \[ [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR18 "Peek K, Versteegh T, Veith S, Whalan M, Edwards S, McKay M, et al. Injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and the incidence of soccer-related head and neck injuries. J Athl Train. 2023;58(6):519–27.")\], and applying these results to female participants should be done cautiously. Given that female athletes are more susceptible to SRCs than male athletes \[ [52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR52 "Van Pelt KL, Allred D, Cameron KL, Campbell DE, D’Lauro CJ, He X, et al. A cohort study to identify and evaluate concussion risk factors across multiple injury settings: findings from the CARE consortium. Injury Epidemiol. 2019;6:1–11.")\] as well as and exhibit a higher number of symptoms and longer durations of symptoms post-injury \[ [53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR53 "Berz K, Divine J, Foss KB, Heyl R, Ford KR, Myer GD. Sex-specific differences in the severity of symptoms and recovery rate following sports-related concussion in young athletes. Physician Sportsmed. 2013;41(2):58–63.")\], more attention and research are needed. Second, the injury prevention programs in the included studies were limited to implementation in three sports: rugby, American Football, and soccer. The educational intervention included in our study was limited to the HUF program, which was specifically designed for American Football. Consequently, our findings may not be generalizable to other sports also with high SRC incidence rates, such as ice hockey and lacrosse \[ [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR30 "Zuckerman SL, Kerr ZY, Yengo-Kahn A, Wasserman E, Covassin T, Solomon GS. Epidemiology of sports-related concussion in NCAA athletes from 2009–2010 to 2013–2014: incidence, recurrence, and mechanisms. Am J Sports Med. 2015;43(11):2654–62.")\]. Third, most of the reviewed studies were not randomized controlled trials (RCTs), as reflected by the low mean score of 7. The lack of randomization introduces potential biases and limits the interpretation of the findings. If feasible and ethically permissible, RCTs should be used as they are the most rigorous method for assessing the efficacy of a prevention program \[ [10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR10 "Emery CA, Pasanen K. Current trends in sport injury prevention. Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol. 2019;33(1):3–15.")\]. Lastly, among the eight included studies, four explicitly used an intention-to-treat (ITT) approach \[ [20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR20 "Attwood MJ, Roberts SP, Trewartha G, England ME, Stokes KA. Efficacy of a movement control injury prevention programme in adult men’s community rugby union: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):368–74."), [22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR22 "Hislop MD, Stokes KA, Williams S, McKay CD, England ME, Kemp SPT, et al. Reducing musculoskeletal injury and concussion risk in schoolboy rugby players with a pre-activity movement control exercise programme: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(15):1140–6."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR26 "Kerr ZY, Yeargin S, Valovich McLeod TC, Nittoli VC, Mensch J, Dodge T, et al. Comprehensive coach education and practice contact restriction guidelines result in lower injury rates in youth American football. Orthop J Sports Med. 2015;3(7):2325967115594578."), [36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR36 "Obërtinca R, Meha R, Hoxha I, Shabani B, Meyer T, Aus der Fünten K. Efficacy of a new injury prevention programme (FUNBALL) in young male football (soccer) players: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2024;58(10):548–55.")\], while the remaining four did not specify whether IRRs were based on ITT or per-protocol (PP) analyses \[ [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR17 "Gillies L, McKay M, Kertanegara S, Huertas N, Nutt S, Peek K. The implementation of a neck strengthening exercise program in elite rugby union: A team case study over one season. Phys Ther Sport. 2022 2022/5//;55:248 – 55."), [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR18 "Peek K, Versteegh T, Veith S, Whalan M, Edwards S, McKay M, et al. Injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and the incidence of soccer-related head and neck injuries. J Athl Train. 2023;58(6):519–27."), [21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR21 "Barden C, Hancock MV, Stokes KA, Roberts SP, McKay CD. Effectiveness of the activate injury prevention exercise programme to prevent injury in schoolboy rugby union. Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(14):812–7."), [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR24 "Shanley E, Thigpen C, Kissenberth M, Gilliland RG, Thorpe J, Nance D, et al. Heads up football training decreases concussion rates in high school football players. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(2):120–6.")\], which may have affected the estimated effect sizes. However, based on the study descriptions, three likely followed an ITT approach \[ [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR17 "Gillies L, McKay M, Kertanegara S, Huertas N, Nutt S, Peek K. The implementation of a neck strengthening exercise program in elite rugby union: A team case study over one season. Phys Ther Sport. 2022 2022/5//;55:248 – 55."), [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR18 "Peek K, Versteegh T, Veith S, Whalan M, Edwards S, McKay M, et al. Injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and the incidence of soccer-related head and neck injuries. J Athl Train. 2023;58(6):519–27."), [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40798-025-00936-4#ref-CR24 "Shanley E, Thigpen C, Kissenberth M, Gilliland RG, Thorpe J, Nance D, et al. Heads up football training decreases concussion rates in high school football players. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(2):120–6.")\]. Therefore, the consistency in analytic methods and the robustness of the pooled estimates support the reliability of the review’s conclusions.

## Conclusion

SRC injury prevention programs could successfully reduce SRC incidence rates by 34% and the efficacy does not vary whether it is physical training or educational intervention as well as in different exposure context. Given the efficacy of both intervention types, healthcare providers and stakeholders can implement these interventions based on their specific contexts to prevent SRC. Further prospective studies are needed to develop injury prevention protocols specifically for female athletes and to explore factors that may influence the efficacy of these interventions, ultimately enhancing the prevention of SRC across various sports.

metadata.dc.description: Sport-related concussions (SRCs) have emerged as a global health concern in sports medicine. Effective injury prevention programs have the potential to reduce the risk of SRCs, but, their efficacy remains inconclusive. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the efficacy of injury prevention programs in preventing SRCs and to examine whether different intervention types (physical- vs. educational-based) and athletic exposure context (practice vs. match) influenced the efficacy of interventions. Six databases (PubMed, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, and Embase databases) were searched in March 2024. Studies were included if (1) the physical training or educational intervention aimed to prevent SRC, (2) the incidence rate (IR) or other outcome data sufficient to calculate the IR for both the intervention and control groups were reported, and (3) the study employed a prospective design. A total of eight studies were included in the analysis, involving 2571 participants (intervention group: n = 1281; control group: n = 1290). Current injury prevention programs primarily targeted male athletes in rugby, American Football, and soccer. The analysis revealed a significant reduction in SRC rate among athletes who received injury prevention programs (incidence rate ratio = 0.66, 95% CI [0.50–0.85], p = .002). The moderator analysis indicated that neither the type of intervention nor the exposure context significantly influenced the efficacy of the injury prevention programs. SRC prevention programs provided a significant protection effect, reducing injury rates by 34%. Importantly, their efficacy remains consistent across both physical training and educational-based programs, as well as in various exposure contexts. However, further prospective studies are needed to develop injury prevention protocols specifically for females and to investigate factors that may influence the efficacy of these interventions to enhance the prevention of SRC across various sports.

A total of eight studies were included in the analysis, involving 2571 participants (intervention group: n = 1281; control group: n = 1290). Current injury prevention programs primarily targeted male athletes in rugby, American Football, and soccer. The analysis revealed a significant reduction in SRC rate among athletes who received injury prevention programs (incidence rate ratio = 0.66, 95% CI [0.50–0.85], p = .002). The moderator analysis indicated that neither the type of intervention nor the exposure context significantly influenced the efficacy of the injury prevention programs. SRC prevention programs provided a significant protection effect, reducing injury rates by 34%. Importantly, their efficacy remains consistent across both physical training and educational-based programs, as well as in various exposure contexts. However, further prospective studies are needed to develop injury prevention protocols specifically for females and to investigate factors that may influence the efficacy of these interventions to enhance the prevention of SRC across various sports.

metadata.og:description: Background Sport-related concussions (SRCs) have emerged as a global health concern in sports medicine. Effective injury prevention programs have the potential to reduce the risk of SRCs, but, their efficacy remains inconclusive. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the efficacy of injury prevention programs in preventing SRCs and to examine whether different intervention types (physical- vs. educational-based) and athletic exposure context (practice vs. match) influenced the efficacy of interventions. Methods Six databases (PubMed, CINAHL, MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, and Embase databases) were searched in March 2024. Studies were included if (1) the physical training or educational intervention aimed to prevent SRC, (2) the incidence rate (IR) or other outcome data sufficient to calculate the IR for both the intervention and control groups were reported, and (3) the study employed a prospective design. Results A total of eight studies were included in the analysis, involving 2571 participants (intervention group: n = 1281; control group: n = 1290). Current injury prevention programs primarily targeted male athletes in rugby, American Football, and soccer. The analysis revealed a significant reduction in SRC rate among athletes who received injury prevention programs (incidence rate ratio = 0.66, 95% CI [0.50–0.85], p = .002). The moderator analysis indicated that neither the type of intervention nor the exposure context significantly influenced the efficacy of the injury prevention programs. Conclusions SRC prevention programs provided a significant protection effect, reducing injury rates by 34%. Importantly, their efficacy remains consistent across both physical training and educational-based programs, as well as in various exposure contexts. However, further prospective studies are needed to develop injury prevention protocols specifically for females and to investigate factors that may influence the efficacy of these interventions to enhance the prevention of SRC across various sports.

Effects of rehabilitation interventions on time to return to play and reinjury rate in athletes with acute hamstring strain injuries


[Download PDF](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1.pdf)

[Download PDF](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1.pdf)

## Abstract

Despite the high prevalence and recurrence of acute hamstring strain injuries in athletes, the optimal rehabilitation strategy balancing rapid time to return to play (TTRTP) with durable re-injury protection remains unclear. We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, and Google Scholar from inception to January 2026 for English-language randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating exercise-based rehabilitation, adjunctive biological modalities, or other approaches for acute hamstring strains in athletes. TTRTP was the primary outcome; re-injury rate was secondary. Certainty was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Models were selected based on heterogeneity and clinical plausibility of pooling. 14 RCTs (693 athletes) were included. A lengthening-focused exercise protocol (L-protocol) based on two trials may shorten TTRTP versus conventional rehabilitation (moderate certainty) without increasing re-injury risk (low certainty). Progressive agility and trunk stabilization (PATS) did not accelerate TTRTP (low certainty); the re-injury estimate was inconclusive (RD -0.35, 95% CI -0.74 to 0.03; I² = 72%; very low certainty; 2 trials), with the confidence interval including both a potential reduction and no effect. For adjunctive therapies, we analyzed Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) as a separate meta-analysis (three trials) and described radial extracorporeal shockwave therapy (rESWT) and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) as single-trial evidence. PRP showed heterogeneous effects (I² = 70%), rESWT modest benefit (one trial), and LLLT no added benefit (one trial). Pain-threshold rehab enhanced strength without delaying TTRTP (moderate certainty; one trial). Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) indicated that the lengthening-focused exercise protocol (L-protocol) TTRTP benefit exceeded the monitoring boundary, suggesting sufficient evidence to rule out random error; however, this does not eliminate clinical heterogeneity or concerns about external validity. Lengthening-focused eccentric exercise may shorten TTRTP. Evidence for PATS and adjunctive modalities remains uncertain, warranting high-quality RCTs. Decisions should prioritize evidence certainty over statistical significance.

Clinical trial registration: PROSPERO registration ID CRD420261387775.

## Introduction

Hamstring strains (HSIs) are one of the most common injuries experienced by athletes in both contact and non-contact sports, with reported frequencies reaching up to 37% in some athletic populations[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR1 "Opar, D. A., Williams, M. D. & Shield, A. J. Hamstring strain injuries. Sports Med. 42, 209–226.                    https://doi.org/10.2165/11594800-000000000-00000                                     (2012)."), [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR2 "Paton, B. M. et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 3: rehabilitation, running and return to sport. Br. J. Sports Med. 57, 278–291.                    https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105384                                     (2023)."), [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR3 "Hagos, A., Merchant, A. A., Kayani, B., Yasen, A. T. & Haddad, F. S. Risk factors and injury prevention strategies for hamstring injuries: a narrative review. EFORT Open. Rev. 10, 636–645.                    https://doi.org/10.1530/EOR-2024-0135                                     (2025)."), [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR4 "Yagiz, G. et al. A retrospective comparison of the biceps femoris long head muscle structure in athletes with and without hamstring strain injury history. PLoS ONE. 19, e0298146.                    https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0298146                                     (2024)."). Similar high injury rates have been observed in physically demanding occupational training, with up to 41% of recruits affected during initial phases[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR5 "Dhahbi, W., Ben Saad, H., Dergaa, I., Souaifi, M. & Chamari, K. Injury profiling in male police cadets during initial training phase: a retrospective cohort study. Am. J. Men’s Health. 18, 15579883241304584.                    https://doi.org/10.1177/15579883241304584                                     (2024)."). Hamstring strains typically occur during movements involving extreme hip flexion and knee extension such as sprinting, jumping, or stretching[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR3 "Hagos, A., Merchant, A. A., Kayani, B., Yasen, A. T. & Haddad, F. S. Risk factors and injury prevention strategies for hamstring injuries: a narrative review. EFORT Open. Rev. 10, 636–645.                    https://doi.org/10.1530/EOR-2024-0135                                     (2025)."). The long head of the biceps femoris (BFlh) is most frequently affected, with injuries typically occurring 0–6 cm proximal to the myotendinous junction[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR1 "Opar, D. A., Williams, M. D. & Shield, A. J. Hamstring strain injuries. Sports Med. 42, 209–226.                    https://doi.org/10.2165/11594800-000000000-00000                                     (2012)."). Acute HSIs present with localized pain and muscle fibre disruption (Grade I-III) of varying severity, which is associated with functional deficits[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR2 "Paton, B. M. et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 3: rehabilitation, running and return to sport. Br. J. Sports Med. 57, 278–291.                    https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105384                                     (2023)."), [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR6 "Huygaerts, S. et al. Mechanisms of hamstring strain injury: interactions between fatigue, muscle activation and function. Sports 8, 65.                    https://doi.org/10.3390/sports8050065                                     (2020)."). This condition is distinct from proximal hamstring tendinopathy (an overuse disorder presenting with chronic deep gluteal pain during loaded activities), tendon avulsions (partial or complete detachment from the ischial tuberosity, often requiring surgical repair), recurrent strains (a repeat injury following an index strain), and delayed-onset posterior-thigh pain (non-traumatic muscle soreness without structural injury). These conditions differ in pathophysiology, natural history, and clinical management[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR1 "Opar, D. A., Williams, M. D. & Shield, A. J. Hamstring strain injuries. Sports Med. 42, 209–226.                    https://doi.org/10.2165/11594800-000000000-00000                                     (2012)."). The high rates of HSIs have persisted for several decades, with some surveillance data indicating an approximate 4% annual increase in incidence in professional football populations[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR7 "Ekstrand, J., Waldén, M. & Hägglund, M. Hamstring injuries have increased by 4% annually in men’s professional football, since 2001: a 13-year longitudinal analysis of the UEFA Elite Club injury study. Br. J. Sports Med. 50, 731–737.                    https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2015-095626                                     (2016)."). HSIs occur more frequently during training than during competition and result in substantial time loss from sport, diminished athletic performance, and considerable economic burden[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR8 "Abdulridha, K. H., Maseer, M. J., Cuenca-Zaldivar, J. N., Aguilar-Latorre, A. & Calatayud, E. Gómez-Soria, I. Comparative effectiveness of rehabilitation protocols for hamstring injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J. Bodyw. Mov. Ther. 44, 820–832.                    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbmt.2025.06.030                                     (2025)."). Additionally, with a recurrence rate of 12–31%, HSIs present a significant challenge for athletes and clinicians alike[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR9 "Dizon, P., Jeanfavre, M., Leff, G. & Norton, R. Comparison of conservative interventions for proximal hamstring tendinopathy: a systematic review and recommendations for rehabilitation. Sports 11, 53.                    https://doi.org/10.3390/sports11030053                                     (2023).").

Physical modalities and therapeutic exercises have been the subject of much research as traditional treatment options for HSIs over the last 20 years[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR10 "Afonso, J. et al. Effectiveness of conservative interventions after acute hamstrings injuries in athletes: a living systematic review. Sports Med. 53, 615–635.                    https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-022-01783-z                                     (2023)."), [11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR11 "Frizziero, A. et al. The role of eccentric exercise in sport injuries rehabilitation. Br. Med. Bull. 110, 47–75.                    https://doi.org/10.1093/bmb/ldu006                                     (2014)."). However, surgical intervention is usually only indicated for more serious or complicated cases[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR12 "Falotico, G. G. & Scatigna, B. F. Surgical repair of proximal hamstring tendon avulsion. Rev. Bras. Ortop. 60, s00451810038.                    https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0045-1810038                                     (2025)."), [13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR13 "Ebrahimi, E., Nourbakhsh, S. A., Sheikhhoseini, R., Mendez-Rebolledo, G. & Mozafari, S. The effect of therapeutic exercises in individuals with joint hypermobility syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Egypt. Rheumatol. Rehabilitation. 53, 38.                    https://doi.org/10.1186/s43166-026-00407-y                                     (2026)."). The overall aim of rehabilitation from an HSI is the safe and timely return to athletic participation while reducing the chance of re-injury. This dual objective restoring function while mitigating recurrence risk is grounded in biomechanical principles that inform both performance optimization and injury prevention strategies. Therefore, clinicians treating athletes must be knowledgeable in evidence-based rehabilitation techniques to provide the athlete with the best possible therapeutic treatments, as well as improve their performance[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR14 "Hickey, J. T., Opar, D. A., Weiss, L. J. & Heiderscheit, B. C. Hamstring strain injury rehabilitation. J. Athl. Train. 57, 125–135 (2022)."), [15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR15 "Marigi, E. M. et al. Hamstring injuries: critical analysis review of current nonoperative treatments. JBJS Rev. 10, e2200095.                    https://doi.org/10.2106/JBJS.RVW.22.00095                                     (2022)."), [16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR16 "Arner, J. W., Rothrauff, B. & Bradley, J. P. Hamstring injuries in athletes: anatomy, pathology, and treatment. J. Am. Acad. Orthop. Surg. 33, e703–e714.                    https://doi.org/10.5435/JAAOS-D-24-01162                                     (2025)."), [17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR17 "Ben Ezzdine, L., Dhahbi, W., Chèze, L. & Editorial Advancing biomechanics: enhancing sports performance, mitigating injury risks, and optimizing athlete rehabilitation, II. Front. Sports Act. Living. 8, 1872907.                    https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2026.1872907                                     (2026).").

A range of adjunctive therapies, including orthobiologics such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and electrophysical agents such as low-level laser therapy (LLLT), radial extracorporeal shockwave therapy (rESWT), capacitive-resistive energy transfer (TECAR) and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), is frequently employed alongside active rehabilitation[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR12 "Falotico, G. G. & Scatigna, B. F. Surgical repair of proximal hamstring tendon avulsion. Rev. Bras. Ortop. 60, s00451810038.                    https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0045-1810038                                     (2025)."), [18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR18 "Sherry, M. A., Johnston, T. S. & Heiderscheit, B. C. Rehabilitation of acute hamstring strain injuries. Clin. Sports Med. 34, 263–284 (2015)."), [19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR19 "Heiderscheit, B. C., Sherry, M. A., Silder, A., Chumanov, E. S. & Thelen, D. G. Hamstring strain injuries: Recommendations for diagnosis, rehabilitation, and injury prevention. J. Orthop. Sports Phys. Ther. 40, 67–81 (2010)."), [20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR20 "Hickey, J. T., Timmins, R. G., Maniar, N., Williams, M. D. & Opar, D. A. Criteria for progressing rehabilitation and determining return-to-play clearance following hamstring strain injury: A systematic review. Sports Med. 47, 1375–1387 (2017)."). However, these interventions differ substantially in their biological rationale, mechanisms of action and clinical objectives, and therefore should not be considered interchangeable[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR21 "Erickson, L. N. & Sherry, M. A. Rehabilitation and return to sport after hamstring strain injury. J. Sport Health Sci. 6, 262–270 (2017)."). PRP has been studied for its potential to deliver growth factors to injured tissue[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR22 "Lee, K. Y., Baker, H. P., Hanaoka, C. M., Tjong, V. K. & Terry, M. A. Treatment of patellar and hamstring tendinopathy with platelet-rich plasma in varsity collegiate athletes: a case series. J. Orthop. 18, 91–94.                    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jor.2019.10.007                                     (2019)."), [23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR23 "Trunz, L. M. et al. Effectiveness of hematoma aspiration and platelet-rich plasma muscle injections for the treatment of hamstring strains in athletes. Med. Sci. Sports Exerc. 54, 12–17.                    https://doi.org/10.1249/MSS.0000000000002758                                     (2022)."). rESWT has been shown to help reduce TTRTP and increase recovery of strength[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR24 "Murat, S., Dogruoz Karatekin, B. & Zengin, M. Clinical and sonographic evaluation of the effectiveness of extracorporeal shock wave therapy in patients with lateral epicondylitis. Medeniyet Med. J. 39, 109–116.                    https://doi.org/10.4274/MMJ.galenos.2024.60308                                     (2024)."). Both TECAR and TENS have been shown to provide better short-term pain relief and improve flexibility than complete rest. However, studies examining the long-term efficacy of these modalities have produced limited data[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR25 "Kelli, A., Apostolou, T., Iakovidis, P., Koutras, G. & Kellis, E. Acute effects of medium-frequency electrical energy transfer (TECAR) and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) on pain and flexibility in athletes with an acute hamstring injury: a randomized controlled trial. Sports Med. Health Sci. 7, 100–108 (2025)."). While physical modalities are used widely, their effectiveness as the sole treatment method is questionable at best; therefore, most studies examined physical modalities as part of a structured exercise program, and therefore the incremental benefit from exercise alone varies greatly by specific modality and stage of injury.

Therapeutic exercise constitutes the cornerstone of HSI rehabilitation, grounded in a strong physiological rationale for restoring muscle strength, flexibility, neuromuscular control, and tissue capacity[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR26 "Liu, H. et al. Knee osteoarthritis rehabilitation: an integrated framework of exercise, nutrition, biomechanics, and physical therapist guidance-a narrative review. Eur. J. Med. Res. 30, 826.                    https://doi.org/10.1186/s40001-025-03083-4                                     (2025)."), [27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR27 "Yagiz, G., Dayala, V. K., Williams, K., Owen, J. A. & Kubis, H. P. Alterations in biceps femoris long head fascicle length, eccentric hamstring strength qualities and single-leg hop distance throughout the ninety minutes of TSAFT90 simulated football match. PLoS ONE. 17, e0278222.                    https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0278222                                     (2022)."). Contemporary exercise-based approaches have shifted from simple stretching and concentric strengthening toward more sophisticated protocols. Eccentric loading, particularly exercises performed at long muscle lengths has gained prominence due to its ability to increase fascicle length and enhance eccentric strength[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR28 "Marušič, J., Vatovec, R., Marković, G. & Šarabon, N. Effects of eccentric training at long-muscle length on architectural and functional characteristics of the hamstrings. Scand. J. Med. Sci. Sports. 30, 2130–2142.                    https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.13770                                     (2020)."). Another approach combines progressive agility exercises with trunk stabilization training (PATS), focusing on lumbopelvic control and movement patterns that mimic sporting actions[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR18 "Sherry, M. A., Johnston, T. S. & Heiderscheit, B. C. Rehabilitation of acute hamstring strain injuries. Clin. Sports Med. 34, 263–284 (2015)."), [29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR29 "Wattananon, P., Sinsurin, K. & Somprasong, S. Association between lumbopelvic motion and muscle activation in patients with non-specific low back pain during forward bending task: a cross-sectional study. Hong Kong Physiother J. 40, 29–37.                    https://doi.org/10.1142/S1013702520500043                                     (2020)."). Stretching exercises have traditionally been incorporated to restore range of motion; however, contemporary evidence suggests that static stretching alone provides limited functional benefit[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR20 "Hickey, J. T., Timmins, R. G., Maniar, N., Williams, M. D. & Opar, D. A. Criteria for progressing rehabilitation and determining return-to-play clearance following hamstring strain injury: A systematic review. Sports Med. 47, 1375–1387 (2017)."), [30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR30 "Copland, S. T., Tipton, J. S. & Fields, K. B. Evidence-based treatment of hamstring tears. Curr. Sports Med. Rep. 8, 308–314.                    https://doi.org/10.1249/JSR.0b013e3181c1d6e1                                     (2009)."), [31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR31 "Dijksma, I. et al. Exercise programs to reduce the risk of musculoskeletal injuries in military personnel: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PM R. 12, 1028–1037.                    https://doi.org/10.1002/pmrj.12360                                     (2020)."). Current guidelines recommend stretching as an adjunct rather than a standalone intervention, with emphasis shifting toward eccentric loading and neuromuscular retraining[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR32 "Hewett, T. E. & Bates, N. A. Preventive biomechanics: a paradigm shift with a translational approach to injury prevention. Am. J. Sports Med. 45, 2654–2664.                    https://doi.org/10.1177/0363546516686080                                     (2017).").

The recent trend in clinical practice and research is towards combining physical modalities with exercise-based rehabilitation[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR33 "Schmitt, B. M., Tyler, T. F., Kwiecien, S. Y., Fox, M. B. & McHugh, M. P. Mapping tenderness to palpation predicts return to play following acute hamstring strain. Int. J. Sports Phys. Ther. 15, 421–428 (2020)."), [34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR34 "Hegyi, A. et al. Validating field methods to estimate the pelvic tilt in sprinting and the relationship between prior hamstring injury and the pelvic tilt in elite female soccer players. J. Hum. Kinet. 98, 17–28.                    https://doi.org/10.5114/jhk/194851                                     (2025)."), on the rationale that physical modalities may modulate pain and inflammation in the acute phase, thereby creating a more favorable environment for early loading[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR35 "Balshaw, T. G. et al. Smaller biceps femoris aponeurosis size in legs with a history of hamstring strain injury. Int. J. Sports Med. 45, 871–883.                    https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2348-2605                                     (2024)."). In contrast, exercise therapy addresses the neuromuscular and biomechanical deficits that predispose athletes to recurrence-deficits that cannot be resolved by physical modalities alone. Preliminary evidence suggests that combined approaches may result in faster recovery than exercise alone, without increasing re-injury risk[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR18 "Sherry, M. A., Johnston, T. S. & Heiderscheit, B. C. Rehabilitation of acute hamstring strain injuries. Clin. Sports Med. 34, 263–284 (2015)."), [19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR19 "Heiderscheit, B. C., Sherry, M. A., Silder, A., Chumanov, E. S. & Thelen, D. G. Hamstring strain injuries: Recommendations for diagnosis, rehabilitation, and injury prevention. J. Orthop. Sports Phys. Ther. 40, 67–81 (2010)."), [36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR36 "Bramah, C., Rhodes, S., Clarke-Cornwell, A. & Dos’Santos, T. Sprint running mechanics are associated with hamstring strain injury: a 6-month prospective cohort study of 126 elite male footballers. Br. J. Sports Med. 60, 178–185.                    https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2024-108600                                     (2026)."). However, the optimal timing, sequencing, and combination of specific modalities with specific exercise protocols remain undefined, primarily due to variability in study design and outcome measures.

Several recent systematic reviews have synthesized evidence on hamstring rehabilitation, but none have provided a stratified synthesis that separates exercise-based interventions from adjunctive therapies rather than pooling them, nor interpreted findings through both GRADE and TSA. This systematic review and meta-analysis therefore aimed to evaluate the efficacy of rehabilitation interventions for acute hamstring strain injuries in athletes, including eccentric loading, PATS and adjunctive biological and physical therapies. The primary outcome was time to return to play; secondary outcomes were re-injury rate, pain and functional recovery. Through this stratified synthesis, we sought to guide clinical decision making by evidence certainty rather than statistical significance alone.

## Methods

This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR37 "Cochrane Collaboration. Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions. (2011).").

### Inclusion criteria

Studies were selected based on the following PICOS criteria. Population: competitive or recreational athletes with acute hamstring strain injuries, diagnosed clinically or by imaging; Intervention: (1) exercise-based rehabilitation programmes (eccentric loading, PATS, stretching); (2) adjunctive biological or physical therapies (PRP, rESWT, LLLT) when combined with structured rehabilitation; (3) stand-alone physical modalities (TECAR, TENS) evaluated as isolated treatments. Stand-alone modalities were included only for narrative synthesis and were not pooled in meta-analyses; Comparison: conventional rehabilitation, placebo, or alternative protocols; Outcomes: TTRTP (primary), re-injury rate, pain, and function (secondary); Study design: published RCTs (English-language only, due to resource constraints; acknowledged in Limitations).

### Exclusion criteria

(1) Unpublished RCTs (including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, cross-sectional studies, observational studies, conference abstracts, case reports or non-randomized controlled trials). One master’s thesis was exceptionally included for narrative synthesis only because it provided unique data on an intervention not covered elsewhere (spinal adjustive therapy); its poor methodological quality (PEDro score 4) is acknowledged in the Limitations and it was not included in any pooled meta-analysis; (2) Studies where participants were not diagnosed with hamstring strain injury; (3) Studies that did not report any training or intervention measures; (4) Studies that did not report at least one of the prespecified outcomes (TTRTP, re-injury rate, pain, or functional outcomes); (5) Studies on chronic tendinopathy, tendon avulsions, or delayed-onset posterior-thigh pain.

### Literature search

The search was conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-70693-1#ref-CR37 "Cochrane Collaboration. Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions. (2011)."). Two reviewers (JZ and SH) independently performed the search and screened all retrieved records. The protocol for this review was registered with PROSPERO in May 2026 (CRD420261387775). The literature search was completed prior to registration, but screening against eligibility criteria and data extraction had not yet commenced. Screening began immediately after registration. The final analytical approach was consistent with the registered protocol, except for the post-hoc disaggregation of physical modalities (PRP, rESWT, LLLT), which is explicitly described in the Results. All other methods (eligibility criteria, outcomes, subgroup categories, analytical models, minimum clinically important difference, GRADE decisions, and TSA analyses) were established before screening began. From database inception to January 2026, PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and Google Scholar databases were searched. The full search strategies for all databases, including controlled vocabulary, free-text terms, Boolean operators, field tags, and limits, are provided in Supplementary Table 1. In addition, three additional records were identified through screening the reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews. All studies were retrieved and imported into the citation database (EndNote 21), and duplicates were removed.
